clue.text: Attractive employment opportunity in testicular enhancement surgery?

blocks.note: plums is the schoolboy slang for testicles
a nose job or a boob job is cosmetic surgery, so the surgery is a job

explanation.walkthrough: 'Job' for cosmetic work is the piece worth banking — nose job, boob job — and the question mark is the setter admitting this particular operation is his own invention.
explanation.definitionFit: a plum job is the pick of the posts going: 'plum' has meant the choicest item since plums were the best bit of the pudding.

clue.text: Afternoon retreats in mountain spot

indicators.note: an army that retreats goes back the way it came, so those two letters are written in the opposite order
the instruction to bury one piece inside the word that follows rather than set it alongside

blocks.note: a mountain of work is a pile of it, and this pile opens after two letters
afternoon is PM on a clock, and it goes in backwards

explanation.walkthrough: A mountain of work is a pile of it — that everyday sense is the step to find, because the clue's mountain is doing its best to look like a real one.
explanation.definitionFit: a pimple is a spot in the skin-blemish sense, the word a teenager uses, rather than a place or a dot.

clue.text: Elevated feeling of empathy is difficult to control

blocks.note: elevated means raised, and raised is up
pity is the fellow feeling you have for someone worse off

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one description of a person, so the seam between the two halves is invisible until you notice that 'elevated' is doing a word's work and not a mood's.
explanation.definitionFit: uppity means getting above yourself and refusing to be told, which is exactly the person a boss calls difficult to control.

clue.text: Liberal judge hates Euro-American national park

indicators.note: a liberal translation is a loose one, bound by no letter of the original, so nothing here has to stay in the order it is given

blocks.note: J is how law reports abbreviate a judge
nine letters taken at face value, thrown in with the J

explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen is the trap. 'Euro' is fodder and 'American' has already crossed over to the definition, where it settles which country's parks are on offer.
explanation.definitionFit: Joshua Tree National Park is a real park in the California desert, so the definition names the class the proper noun belongs to.

clue.text: Item to assist washing behind ears trialled initially under offer

indicators.note: at the outset — so only the letter each word starts with is taken
places one piece below the other, and in a down entry below means later along the answer

blocks.note: an offer at auction is a bid
the letters those two words start with

explanation.walkthrough: Everything turns on where 'behind' belongs: the surface has you scrubbing behind your ears, and the definition means the other behind entirely.
explanation.definitionFit: a bidet is the low bathroom basin you sit astride to wash your bottom, so the definition names it by the job it does.

clue.text: Burglar in Shoreditch that’s likely to end up in hot water

definitions.text: likely to end up in hot water

blocks.note: Cockney rhyming slang, spoken in Shoreditch, supplies a two-word term for a burglar built to rhyme with thief

blocks.clueFragment: likely to end up in hot water
blocks.note: the flat literal reading — what goes into the pot once the kettle has boiled

explanation.walkthrough: 'In hot water' works both halves at once: trouble for the burglar, and the teapot for the leaf.
explanation.definitionFit: tea leaf is the Cockney rhyme for thief, and the same two words also name the literal leaf that gets brewed, so the phrase carries both senses.

clue.text: Brief violent disturbance in match report? That is probably exaggerated

indicators.note: brief means cut short, so the word it governs arrives a letter shorter than it should be
says one piece is planted inside the other rather than laid beside it

blocks.note: figures that tally are figures that match, and this one splits before its last letter
a storm is a violent disturbance, docked of its final M

explanation.walkthrough: 'Match' looks like the game and is really the verb, the one figures do when they agree — which is the step the scuffle-at-a-match surface exists to hide.
explanation.definitionFit: a tall story is an account stretched well past the truth, so the definition is the whole idiom rather than a synonym for either word in it.

clue.text: Discovered wildlife trip a long way away

indicators.note: read it as dis-covered, stripped of its covering, so the letters wrapped round the outside come off

blocks.note: a safari is a trip to see wildlife; lose the S at the front and the I at the back

explanation.walkthrough: 'Discovered' is a lovely piece of misdirection — it looks like a past tense reporting a find, and it is an instruction to take the wrapping off.
explanation.definitionFit: afar survives mainly in the phrase 'from afar', where it means at a great distance, which is what 'a long way away' says plainly.

clue.text: Prepared cod pies, eating one from time to time

definitions.note: 'From time to time' is an adverbial phrase where the answer is an adjective; the setter is defining the pattern of occurrence rather than matching the grammar.

indicators.note: food that has been prepared has been chopped and mixed, so nothing stays in the state it arrived in
what is eaten goes inside, so that letter is swallowed into the mixture

blocks.note: seven letters taken at face value, not as words
one is the Roman numeral I, the commonest single letter in the language of clues

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a cook at work, which is exactly what an anagram indicator wants to look like — 'prepared' sounds like an account of dinner rather than an order.
explanation.definitionFit: something episodic happens in separate bursts with gaps in between, which is occasional rather than continuous — the pattern 'from time to time' describes.

clue.text: Trump's trousers in English painting?

definitions.note: Painting is one of the fine arts and the answer names the whole plural family, so the question mark is the setter flagging an example rather than a synonym.

indicators.note: to trouser something is to pocket it, to take it inside, so the word before swallows what comes after

blocks.note: to trump is to break wind, so this reads as the verb trumps
taken at face value, two letters of the filling
E is the standard abbreviation for English

explanation.walkthrough: The politician is a decoy: nothing about this Trump is a surname, and once the word turns into a verb the trousers stop being clothing and become a hiding place.
explanation.definitionFit: the fine arts are those practised for beauty rather than use — painting, sculpture, music — so the clue offers one member of that group.

clue.text: Roaming Epsom Downs

indicators.note: something roaming keeps to no fixed route, so its letters are free to wander into another order

blocks.note: five letters taken as letters, not as a town

explanation.walkthrough: Epsom Downs is the racecourse, which is the entire trick: two words that name one place are really fodder and definition standing next to each other.
explanation.definitionFit: 'the mopes' is an old plural noun for a fit of low spirits, so it answers 'downs' in the ups-and-downs sense rather than the hills.

clue.text: Matilda reworked by an Adriatic resident

indicators.note: a thing reworked has been taken apart and made again in another shape, which is what happens to these letters

blocks.note: the italics mark a title, and titles are fair fodder
two more letters joining the mix, doing no grammatical work at all

explanation.walkthrough: 'An' looks like the article introducing the definition, which is why it is easy to leave out of the count — and the anagram is two letters short without it.
explanation.definitionFit: Dalmatia is the Croatian coast of the Adriatic, so a Dalmatian is a person who lives there; the spotted dog is the same word's other sense.

clue.text: Touchstone's requirement to be inspired by working titles

indicators.note: worked in the sense dough is worked, kneaded into a different shape rather than employed
to inspire is literally to breathe in, so whatever is inspired ends up inside the other piece

blocks.note: the six letters of 'titles' kneaded into a new order, which then parts after three
a requirement is a must

explanation.walkthrough: Touchstone is also the clown in As You Like It, so the apostrophe-s reads as his possession when it is really standing in for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: a touchstone was the dark stone a jeweller rubbed gold against to assay it, so both words name a single trial that settles a question outright.

clue.text: What could follow on from club's spinning difficulties

definitions.text: What could follow on from club

indicators.note: a thing spinning comes round to face the other way, so the letters are read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: an ado is a fuss or a difficulty, and the plural gives four letters to turn

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is pure cricket — 'follow on' and 'spinning' both belong to the game — while the answer is behind the bar.
explanation.definitionFit: club soda is the bar-trade name for fizzy water, so the definition points at the phrase the answer completes rather than at any meaning of its own.

clue.text: Separating from Esther? The woman's away and phoned up during golf!

indicators.note: the woman is HER, and 'away' is the order to take those three letters out of the name in front

blocks.note: drop the HER from ESTHER, minus the woman, and EST is what stays
to ring someone up is to phone them
during and in are the same preposition of time
golf is the radio alphabet's word for G, alongside alpha and bravo

explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark sells the surface as gossip on a fairway, which is why nobody looks at 'golf' and sees a single letter of the radio alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: to estrange is to drive people apart until they stop speaking, so the -ing form matches 'separating' in the sense of a relationship coming apart.

clue.text: A flirty swot developed into international chart topper

indicators.note: grown into something else, so the fodder does not keep the shape it arrives in

blocks.note: eleven letters taken at face value, the whole phrase and nothing else

explanation.walkthrough: A living person's name is fair game as an answer, and the surface — a schoolgirl who turned out well — is doing all the work of hiding a phrase that is already in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: her albums go to number one in country after country, so the definition is by example: one named artist standing in for the description.

clue.text: It's your turn, we're told, to toil endlessly ahead of South Balkans race

definitions.note: 'Race' is a singular collective while the answer is the plural that names its members, a mismatch setters allow when the word means a people.

indicators.note: reported speech: take the words as they sound rather than as they are spelt
without its end, so the last letter of the word never arrives
puts the piece in front of what follows rather than behind it

blocks.note: if it is your turn then you go, and 'you go' said aloud is written this way
to slave is to toil, and the final E never gets said
S is the compass abbreviation for south

explanation.walkthrough: A whole country is buried in the pun: the first four letters are nothing but two everyday words heard rather than read, which is why they look like a foreign spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: the Yugoslavs were the peoples of the federation that occupied much of the Balkans, so 'race' is doing its loose sense of a nation's people.

clue.text: Site manager detailed ineffective medication

definitions.note: 'Medication' is a mass noun covering any number of pills, so it fairly defines a plural answer without itself being one.

indicators.note: read as de-tailed, robbed of its tail, so the word in front loses its last letter

blocks.note: the site of something is the place it happens
a manager is a BOSS, and the tail comes off

explanation.walkthrough: 'Detailed' is the whole clue in one word: it reads as an adjective describing thorough paperwork and works as a verb meaning docked.
explanation.definitionFit: a placebo is the dummy pill given to a trial's control group, so 'ineffective medication' names it by the very thing it deliberately lacks.

clue.text: Academician put in danger rings London college

indicators.note: to ring something is to draw a circle round it, so one piece closes about the other

blocks.note: to imperil someone is to put them in danger, and the word opens before its last letter
A is the abbreviation for an Academician

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rings' looks like a verb about telephones sitting between two nouns, which is what keeps the sentence upright while it quietly gives an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Imperial College is one of London University's science institutions, so the definition names the place by category and leaves you to supply the name.

clue.text: Perhaps chicken crosses major road to join vulture

indicators.note: what crosses something lies over it from side to side, so this word ends up on both sides of what follows

blocks.note: a hen kept for eggs is a layer, and 'perhaps' owns up that not every chicken is one
M is what a motorway is numbered with — the M1, the M25
traffic joining a road merges with it

explanation.walkthrough: The oldest joke in the book is doing the work here: the chicken really does cross the road, and it is the wordplay rather than the punchline.
explanation.definitionFit: the lammergeyer is the bearded vulture of Alpine and Himalayan crags, so 'vulture' names the family this particular bird belongs to.

clue.text: Party hire for merchant banks

indicators.note: to bank something is to stow it away for safe keeping, so the letters are being kept inside the words around them

blocks.note: the letters run unbroken across hiRE FOR Merchant, straddling three words

explanation.walkthrough: 'Merchant banks' is the least suspicious pair of words in the clue, which is exactly why the answer is lying across them.
explanation.definitionFit: Reform is the name of a British political party, so 'Party' identifies the word as a proper noun rather than defining what it means.

clue.text: Ban on sailing vessels turning up and dropping off children is to remain after all

indicators.note: a down entry read from the bottom comes up the grid, so the letters are written in reverse
something dropping off falls away and is gone, which is what happens to the pair named next to it

blocks.note: a ban is a flat no
ch is the abbreviation for children, and this is the pair that falls away
sailing vessels are YACHTS, and without that CH you are left with YATS

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is the school run — dropping children off — while every one of those words is really an instruction. Only 'up' tells you the assembly is read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: to stay on is to remain when everyone else has left, as a teacher stays on past retirement, so 'after all' means after all the rest have gone.

clue.text: Champ in essentially atrocious shape

indicators.note: the essence of a word is at its very centre, so only the letter in the middle is wanted

blocks.note: the fifth of its nine letters, with four on either side
to hew is to shape stone or timber by cutting it

explanation.walkthrough: 'In' reads as a preposition and is only joinery, which leaves 'essentially' looking like an adverb of emphasis rather than the instruction it is.
explanation.definitionFit: to champ is to chew noisily — the horse's word, as in champing at the bit — which is why the plain synonym feels old-fashioned.

clue.text: Die-cast ring entrepreneur imports acid

indicators.note: to import is to carry something in from outside, so the words are carrying the answer inside themselves

blocks.note: the letters run unbroken from the middle of the first word: die-cASTRINGENTrepreneur

explanation.walkthrough: Ten letters is a long thing to hide, and the hyphen helps by breaking your eye exactly one letter before the answer starts.
explanation.definitionFit: an astringent taste is sharp and puckering, which is 'acid' used of flavour rather than of chemistry.

clue.text: Where lurchers rounded, guarding the King?

indicators.note: turned about, so the buried letters are read from the far end back to the near one
to guard something is to keep it safe within your own walls, so these words are holding a word inside them

blocks.note: the letters sit unbroken across wheRE LURchers, waiting to be read the other way

explanation.walkthrough: A lurcher is a poacher's crossbred dog, which is why 'Where lurchers' reads as a place to look for one rather than as a hiding place.
explanation.definitionFit: a king is one kind of ruler, so the question mark marks a definition by example — the class named by one of its members.

clue.text: Read superficially, Jagger's missing constant "rolling"

indicators.note: what is missing has gone, so the letter named beside it is not in the answer
letters set rolling come to rest in a different order, and Jagger's own band name is what makes the word look innocent here

blocks.note: Jagger is Mick, so his name plus the S of 'Jagger's' gives five letters
c is the physicist's constant, the speed of light, and it is the letter that goes

explanation.walkthrough: Quotation marks around a word are usually the setter pointing at it, and here they point at a Rolling Stone: 'rolling' is the instruction and the joke at once.
explanation.definitionFit: to skim a page is to take in only its surface, catching the gist and none of the detail.

clue.text: Barrier erected as a result of Spooner's fight in Northern Scotland

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of two words, so naming him is the order to trade them over

blocks.note: Wick is the town on the far north coast of Scotland, and it takes in the BR the other word gives up
a brawl is a fight, and it hands its BR over in exchange for the W

explanation.walkthrough: Spooner clues stand or fall on the place name, and this one is a real town rather than a region — the north of Scotland has only so many.
explanation.definitionFit: a brick wall is the immovable barrier of the idiom, the thing you hit when progress stops dead.

clue.text: Heard why seaweed from the East is rich in essential element

indicators.note: asks for the word as your ear takes it rather than as the page spells it
what comes from the east travels westward, so in an across entry the letters run right to left

blocks.note: say the letter Y aloud and you have said 'why'
nori is the seaweed sushi is wrapped in, which is why 'from the East' reads as its origin

explanation.walkthrough: Everything in the clue is pointing east — the seaweed, the direction — and the direction is the only word doing cryptic work.
explanation.definitionFit: irony is also the adjective from iron, meaning full of it, and iron is an element the body must have, so the sarcasm sense never comes into it.

clue.text: Setter is regrettably backing square sausages

indicators.note: going the other way, so everything named before it is written from right to left

blocks.note: the setter is the person who wrote the clue, so 'setter is' is I'm
alas is the word you say when reporting something regrettably
S abbreviates square, as in a street address

explanation.walkthrough: Setter means the person writing, not the dog and not the sun — one of the first conventions worth owning, since it turns up in every puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: salami is the cured Italian sausage, and the plural covers several of them or several varieties, which is what 'sausages' asks for.

clue.text: Government trimmed part of the army

indicators.note: trimming takes a little off the end, so the word beside it arrives one letter short

blocks.note: a regiment is the army unit, and its last letter is what gets trimmed

explanation.walkthrough: Regime and regimen are close cousins from the same Latin root, so the definition sounds like a typo until you remember a regimen is a rule you live by.
explanation.definitionFit: regimen carries the old sense of rule or government — the same idea as the regimen a doctor governs your diet with.
